item.text: I’ll read the seven parts in order, place the new notes against the existing questions, then write the update and run the checker.

item.aggregated_output:
<<18:19 update 2, part 0 of 0..6>>
## THE CURRENT MAP
18:19/q01 What does 'thus' compare the awakening with? [وَكَذَٰلِكَ · links] (turns on: Whether the demonstrative recalls the preceding sleep or heightens the new event.)
  18:19/q01/p1 God's preceding sleep and preservation of the youths, equally wondrous signs of His power. — reasons: Al-Wahidi links sleep, increased guidance and turning (18:11,13,18); al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari compare the sleep; al-Baghawi and al-Tabrisi stress preservation from decay; Abu Hayyan sees the earlier compressed account; Alusi says both display overwhelming power.
  18:19/q01/p2 The awakening is likened to itself to magnify its wonder. — reasons: Ibn Ashur compares the rhetorical usage at 2:143. Ibn Qutayba's general account of Arabic exaggeration says understood meanings may be expressed through seemingly impossible events; his poetic evidence includes trees throwing or standing for crowds, Suhayl spoiling wine, night taking the sun's soul, star-drinking camels and spiders aging in hair.
18:19/q02 What does 'We raised them' mean and how were they raised? [بَعَثْنَٰهُمْ · meaning] (turns on: Whether baʿth is read as bodily awakening in the account or as an inward state.)
  18:19/q02/p1 God woke or revived them from a deathlike long sleep, with their bodies and condition preserved. — reasons: Abu Ubayda relates baʿth to resurrection; Ibn Qutayba and al-Wahidi compare slumber to death; Jishumi gives its root as stirring and its other uses as sending messengers or raising the dead; al-Qurtubi cites a poet's waking usage. Ibn Kathir says skin and hair were unchanged after 309 years; al-Asamm and al-Qurtubi say they woke as they slept. Al-Damghānī gives sending a messenger or dispatching someone as another sense of baʿth, citing 62:2 and 2:129.
  18:19/q02/p2 The awakening is an inward return to wakefulness or sobriety. — reasons: Qashani calls it the Sufi first awakening, in which faculties discuss latent meanings; Alusi reports the return from spiritual intoxication.
18:19/q03 Why were they awakened to question one another? [لِيَتَسَآءَلُوا۟ بَيْنَهُمْ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the lām marks a direct purpose or a consequence, and which wisdom the dialogue serves.)
  18:19/q03/p1 Their questioning was a purpose of the awakening, revealing God's power and the duration's mystery. — reasons: Muqatil and Jishumi take the stated end directly; al-Razi says disclosure of divine power is desirable itself; al-Samin prefers causal purpose; Tabatabai ties it to 18:12 and rejects reducing it to a minor consequence; Ibn Ashur says it benefits the youths by direct knowledge of resurrection, like Abraham in 2:260. Al-Biqai adds faith and certainty; al-Tabrisi adds recognition of the Creator and gratitude.
  18:19/q03/p2 Questioning was the resulting event, while the awakening chiefly displayed divine power. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi read the lām as consequence, citing 28:8; al-Baghawi calls questioning an outcome; al-Khafaji prefers this because divine power is the purpose; Asad renders it 'and they began to ask.' Al-Samin and Tabatabai argue against this reduction.
  18:19/q03/p3 They questioned one another to determine their condition, reflect, grow certain and give thanks. — reasons: Al-Tabari says the long sleep seemed strange; al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, and al-Baydawi treat the event as a sign of sleep and resurrection; Elmalili says self-knowledge is a primary concern.
18:19/q04 How is the questioning dialogue introduced? [قَالَ قَآئِلٌۭ مِّنْهُمْ · grammar]
  18:19/q04/p1 The quoted question explains the preceding statement that they questioned one another. — reasons: Alusi calls the introductory qāla a resumption; Ibn Ashur calls the ensuing dialogue an explanation of tasāʾul, mutual questioning. Sībawayh treats established Arabic formulas as independent utterances governed by usage: salām and wayl expressions cannot be freely replaced; he cites 13:29 for a raised construction, 83:1 and 77:34 for a doom statement, 9:30 for ordinary idiom, and gives appositional, adjectival and separate-accusative parses of a repeated wayl.
18:19/q05 Who asked 'How long did you stay?' [قَآئِلٌۭ مِّنْهُمْ · referent] (turns on: The narrative does not name the questioner; transmitted identifications differ.)
  18:19/q05/p1 Their leader Maksalmina, also spelled Miksalmina, asked. — reasons: Muqatil calls him eldest; al-Tha'labi, al-Baghawi, Bursevi and others call him chief; Alusi and Abu Hayyan preserve alternatives.
  18:19/q05/p2 An unnamed member asked, apparently sensing an unusual interval. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya cites signs of an extraordinary sleep; Tabatabai suggests its heaviness; al-Biqai suggests appearance or other signs.
  18:19/q05/p3 Tamlikha or Yamlikha, the youth who managed or carried the provisions, asked. — reasons: Abu Hayyan and Alusi transmit this alternative; the name has spelling variants.
  18:19/q05/p4 Taksalmina asked how long they had stayed. — reasons: Al-Itqān names Taksalmina as the questioner.
18:19/q06 Why did they ask how long they had stayed? [كَمْ لَبِثْتُمْ · interpretation] (turns on: The notes give different motives and scope for the question.)
  18:19/q06/p1 They noticed something unusual and sought to gauge the sleep's duration. — reasons: Al-Tabari says it seemed strange; Ibn Atiyya says conditions looked similar enough that a sudden change was unlikely; al-Biqai points to appearance or other signs, Tabatabai to the heaviness of sleep; al-Tha'labi notes their surprise.
  18:19/q06/p2 They feared they had missed a prayer. — reasons: Al-Tha'labi, al-Baghawi and Alusi record the concern.
  18:19/q06/p3 The question asks how long since they entered the cave. — reasons: Ibn Abbas states this construal.
18:19/q07 How is 'how long' parsed? [كَمْ لَبِثْتُمْ · grammar]
  18:19/q07/p1 Kam is an accusative time expression with 'days' understood. — reasons: Al-Tabrisi supplies the omitted counted unit from the answer; al-Samin calls it adverbial.
18:19/q08 How is labithtum pronounced? [لَبِثْتُمْ · readings] (turns on: Whether thāʾ remains distinct or assimilates into the following consonant.)
  18:19/q08/p1 The other four readers assimilate thāʾ; proximity of articulation permits the form. — reasons: Ibn Mujahid reports the four; al-Nahhas explains that the articulation points are close.
  18:19/q08/p2 Ibn Kathir, Nafi and Asim pronounce thāʾ distinctly. — reasons: Ibn Mujahid names the three readers and says this occurs in each form of the word.
18:19/q09 How should 'a day or part of a day' be understood? [لَبِثْنَا يَوْمًا أَوْ بَعْضَ يَوْمٍۢ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether aw expresses one uncertain estimate, a correction, or different speakers; one report gives longer guesses.)
  18:19/q09/p1 The group gave an uncertain estimate, first thinking a day and then part of one. — reasons: Morning entry and remaining sunlight explain the revision for Muqatil, Yahya, al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Tabrisi and others. Alusi favors plain doubt over a correction; Tabatabai says one speaker's uncertain estimate and rejects distributed speakers. Ibn Kathir says they later deferred to God. Al-Burhān's discussion of wishing distinguishes desire for an outcome from love and debates which particles can mark prospective and past senses; this gives general grammatical background to a speaker's uncertain estimate, without determining the duration.
  18:19/q09/p2 Different youths supplied the two estimates: some said a day, others part of one. — reasons: Al-Nahhas transmits Ibn Abbas with separate youths; Abu Hayyan allows aw to distribute the answers; Elmalili reads the two groups similarly; Ibn Ashur allows it. Alusi calls distribution unlikely; Tabatabai rejects it.
  18:19/q09/p3 The report has one day, two days, or longer. — reasons: Ibn Abbas report in al-Durr and Tabatabai; Tabatabai objects that two days or more conflicts with the Quranic wording and ordinary evidence.
18:19/q10 Why did their estimate seem so short, and what later made them doubt it? [يَوْمًا أَوْ بَعْضَ يَوْمٍۢ · interpretation] (turns on: The sources differ on the immediate cue for the short guess and on the later evidence of elapsed time.)
  18:19/q10/p1 They slept from morning until later daylight, so the visible sun made a day or part of one seem plausible. — reasons: Yahya, Muqatil, al-Wahidi and many others describe morning entry and late waking; al-Kashifi places waking around afternoon, which Bursevi favors because a shopping round trip needed daylight. Alusi says sleep haze prevented checking signs.
  18:19/q10/p2 Their grown hair and nails, or altered faces, suggested a much longer sleep. — reasons: Al-Tha'labi, al-Baghawi, al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Study Quran mention the signs; Ibn Jawzi reports them as an alternative. Kashshaf juxtaposes these signs with the morning account.
  18:19/q10/p3 Sleep and inward absorption disrupt the ability to measure elapsed time. — reasons: Al-Baydawi says sleepers cannot measure duration; al-Qushayri says absorption removed self-awareness; Alusi says sleep haze; Tabatabai notes shadows and sunlight cannot fix an exact day and external events require indicators. Al-Damghānī's lexical heading lists falling and cessation or interruption among senses of zawāl; the excerpt does not develop those senses.
18:19/q11 Who said that their Lord knew best how long they had stayed? [قَالُوا۟ رَبُّكُمْ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا لَبِثْتُمْ · referent] (turns on: The repeated qālū may introduce another group, the whole group, a named leader, or divine speech.)
  18:19/q11/p1 A different group of youths corrected those who estimated a day. — reasons: Al-Tabari says the others deferred; al-Zamakhshari says evidence or inspiration showed them a long stay; Abu Hayyan prefers two groups from the dialogue. Alusi says this fits its question-and-answer structure; Tabatabai says they had deeper monotheistic insight, distinct from the factions of 18:12.
  18:19/q11/p2 Their leader Maksalmin
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<18:19 update 2, part 1 of 0..6>>
a, the eldest, stopped the dispute. — reasons: Muqatil names him; al-Mawardi cites Ibn Abbas; al-Tha'labi and al-Baghawi transmit this explanation; Ibn Jawzi records the name as Miksalmina.
  18:19/q11/p3 Tamlikha or Yamlikha, described as their leader, gave the answer. — reasons: Al-Wahidi cites Ibn Abbas; al-Tabrisi and al-Razi cite him as the leader, with al-Razi saying altered hair, nails and faces led him to infer a long period. Ibn Jawzi records a competing name. Al-Itqān identifies Tamlikhā as leader and the speaker who said God knew the duration.
  18:19/q11/p4 The whole group agreed to defer to God, or one person's accepted answer was attributed to all. — reasons: Ibn Ashur gives both possibilities; al-Baghawi reports the group statement; al-Biqai sees affectionate agreement. Alusi disfavors the same speaker giving both answers.
  18:19/q11/p5 It is God's own statement about their duration. — reasons: Al-Mawardi records this alternative to speech by the youths.
18:19/q12 What does deferring their duration to God express? [رَبُّكُمْ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا لَبِثْتُمْ · theology] (turns on: The ordinary explanation concerns epistemic humility; the inward account treats time itself differently.)
  18:19/q12/p1 They acknowledge that only God knows the exact, long duration, and end an unresolvable dispute. — reasons: Muqatil says Maksalmina returns the matter to God; al-Qushayri says God placed them in that state; al-Kashshaf says signs or inspiration may have exposed their ignorance; al-Biqai calls it faithful fellowship; Tabatabai contrasts human inference from indicators with God's direct encompassing knowledge (96:5; 2:32). Sībawayh explains the hope in 20:44 as belonging to Moses and Aaron, whose knowledge of the outcome was limited; this supplies a parallel for speech limited to human knowledge.
  18:19/q12/p2 A leader urged them to stop disagreement because it can ruin a community. — reasons: Al-Nahhas transmits Ibn Abbas through Sa'id b. Jubayr; al-Durr repeats the leader's warning.
  18:19/q12/p3 Some spiritually realized sleepers understood that the interval had no independent reality. — reasons: Asad connects this to 18:12 and death and resurrection.
18:19/q13 How many youths does the dialogue imply? [قَالَ قَآئِلٌۭ مِّنْهُمْ قَالُوا۟ · interpretation]
  18:19/q13/p1 At least seven: one asks and two plural replies require three speakers each. — reasons: Al-Nasafi attributes the inference to Ibn Abbas; Tabatabai gives the same count from the singular and two plurals.
18:19/q14 Why do they turn from duration to sending for food? [فَٱبْعَثُوٓا۟ أَحَدَكُم · interpretation] (turns on: Both hunger and fear shape the errand.)
  18:19/q14/p1 They woke hungry and redirected an unknowable discussion to an immediate need. — reasons: Al-Tabari says they needed food; al-Kashshaf, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur call the pivot wiser than continuing debate; al-Qushayri says hunger followed a period without bodily appetites; Alusi points to fa as marking the redirect. Al-Rāzī's general account distinguishes ends desired in themselves from means, assigns appetite its own pleasure, and says perceived pleasure draws action unless a stronger consideration intervenes; his examples include tasty food avoided for harm and immediate pain accepted to escape worse harm.
  18:19/q14/p2 The errand also let the envoy learn news about their pursuers. — reasons: Al-Tabari and al-Tha'labi report instructions to buy more food and investigate; they still believed Decianus sought them.
18:19/q15 Who was sent to the city? [أَحَدَكُم · referent] (turns on: Narrative reports name the envoy; the verse leaves him unnamed.)
  18:19/q15/p1 Yamlikha, also called Tamlikha, was the envoy. — reasons: Muqatil names Yamliha; al-Tabari transmits Muqatil and narrative forms; al-Tha'labi, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and others give variants. Al-Ghaznawi calls him the youngest; al-Wahidi has their leader Tamlikha speak earlier. Al-Damghānī names the envoy Malyakhā; al-Itqān names him Tamlikhā.
  18:19/q15/p2 An unnamed member of their group went; the command need not identify him. — reasons: Ibn Ashur says the group may address an unspecified delegate or omit the known name; the Quran's 'one of you' emphasizes membership.
  18:19/q15/p3 The wording 'one of you' avoids suggesting a specially honored chief. — reasons: Ibn al-Anbari contrasts aḥad with wāḥid; Alusi says the latter might imply their chief. Abū Ḥātim supplies wider lexical reasons for the choice of aḥad over wāḥid: its scope, gender invariance, collective possibility and restricted arithmetic use.
18:19/q16 How does 'with your silver' attach to the envoy? [بِوَرِقِكُمْ · grammar]
  18:19/q16/p1 It is circumstantial to 'one of you': the envoy goes carrying the silver. — reasons: Al-Samin describes the prepositional phrase as a circumstantial qualifier.
18:19/q17 What occupations do reports give the youths? [بِوَرِقِكُمْ · reports]
  18:19/q17/p1 They were money changers. — reasons: Abu Ja'far's report calls them money changers; al-Sadiq distinguishes changers in speech from dealers in coins.
18:19/q18 What is 'your silver'? [بِوَرِقِكُمْ · meaning] (turns on: Whether the noun denotes silver generally or minted coins in its lexical scope.)
  18:19/q18/p1 Silver, whether struck as dirhams or unminted; in context it was their money. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba and later authors cite the Arfaja silver-nose report to show unminted silver is included. Al-Asma'i's paper-leaf explanation is dismissed by Alusi. Al-Mawardi distinguishes a fatḥa livestock sense attested in poetry. Biqai develops a lexical family involving foliage, beauty, wealth and gathering; Islahi accordingly translates 'currency.'
  18:19/q18/p2 Specifically coined silver dirhams. — reasons: The wording and old coin reports support a struck currency; Ibn Ashur calls it a minted coin; several authors describe the king's stamped image. Alusi reports this narrower common explanation.
18:19/q19 How is bi-wariqikum read? [بِوَرِقِكُمْ · readings] (turns on: The variants concern vowel easing and the qāf-kāf contact; sources disagree on which assimilations are sound.)
  18:19/q19/p1 Fatḥa on wāw and sukūn on rāʾ lightens pronunciation. — reasons: Al-Farra names Asim and al-A'mash; most Kufans/Basrans, Abu Amr, Hamza and Abu Bakr are often named. Ibn Khalawayh, al-Nahhas and Qiraat-Er explain avoiding a heavy sequence of vowels. Ibn al-Jazarī names Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza, Khalaf, Abū Bakr and Rawḥ as leaving the rāʾ of biwariqikum unvocalized.
  18:19/q19/p2 Assimilation of qāf into kāf, sometimes with a still rāʾ, is transmitted. — reasons: Al-Tabari reports a Meccan form; al-Zajjaj permits it and al-Farisi explains movement from the rear qāf to nearer kāf. Abu Hatim transmits Ibn Muhaysin; Ibn Jinni says possible, yet calls Abu Raja's form concealed articulation rather than full assimilation because full assimilation transfers the vowel. Abu Hayyan challenges a reported attribution to Ibn Kathir. Ibn al-Jazarī reports two valid treatments of a quiescent qāf before kāf: Makkī retains its emphatic quality, while al-Dānī assimilates fully; Ibn al-Jazarī favors the latter by analogy with a moving qāf and warns against weakening an unassimilated qāf. He limits within-word qāf-to-kāf assimilation to forms with a moving preceding letter and following plural mīm.
  18:19/q19/p3 Fatḥa on wāw and kasra on rāʾ, with qāf pronounced, is the common or original reading. — reasons: Al-Tabari prefers the original kasra pattern but accepts alternatives; Ibn Khalawayh calls kasra original. Ibn Mujahid, al-Farisi, al-Qurtubi and others name Ibn Kathir, Nafi, Ibn Amir, al-Kisa'i and Hafs; al-Tabari lists Medinan and some Iraqi readers. The forms are Arabic dialect variants with the same sense. Ibn al-Jazarī explicitly lists biwariqikum among forms where qāf is pronounced distinctly, because its preceding letter is quiescent; he reports kasra on rāʾ for the remaining readers.
  18:19/q19/p4 Kasra on wāw, with varying rāʾ and assimilation, is a rare dialectal reading. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj judges kasra wāw least acceptable; al-Farra compares kibid and kalima. Ibn Jinni treats Abu Raja's form as concealed articulation; Zamakhshari and Razi object to two consecutive still letters in Ibn Muhaysin's form; Abu Hayyan cites a nonassimilated Zajjaj form.
  18:19/q19/p5 Ali reads bawāriqikum, a collective form relating to silver. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Samin describe its pattern; Alusi mentions it.
18:19/q20 What does the demonstrative 'this' add to the silver? [بِوَرِقِكُمْ هَٰذِهِۦٓ · rhetoric]
  18:19/q20/p1 It points to money at hand, perhaps held out or handed to the envoy. — reasons: Bursevi infers a companion physically handed it over; Alusi says the speaker held it out. Tabatabai says the unusually emphatic mention foreshadows how the aged coin exposed them. Sībawayh observes that an identified person may be indicated by a bare proper name when a visible sign reveals him, as if 'this' were uttered; this supplies a general Arabic parallel for demonstrative pointing.
18:19/q21 What were the coins like and where had they come from? [بِوَرِقِكُمْ هَٰذِهِۦٓ · reports] (turns on: Narratives add the old ruler's imprint to the verse's bare mention of silver.)
  18:19/q21/p1 They carried old coins from the reign they fled, often bearing the persecuting king's image. — reasons: Al-Wahidi and Ibn Abbas say the stamped image was the old king's; al-Tabari dates the coins 309 years earlier; al-Tha'labi says Daqyanus' seal. Ibn Kathir says they brought and spent money when fleeing; Abu Hayyan says they brought it for expenses. Ibn Abbas likens the currency to camel hooves; later reports call the ruler Decius.
  18:19/q21/p2 Their coin was silver but its exact minting is not specified by the verse. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba, al-Kashshaf and al-Razi allow coined and uncoined silver; al-Wahidi cites the old stamped-coin narrative as a separate report.
18:19/q22 Which city was meant? [ٱلْمَ
<<part 1 ends; continues in part 2>>

<<18:19 update 2, part 2 of 0..6>>
دِينَةِ · referent] (turns on: Reports vary in names and whether they denote one city over time.)
  18:19/q22/p1 Their former city was Ephesus, also reported as Daqsus or Daphsus and later called Tarsus. — reasons: Al-Tabari calls it Ephesus; al-Wahidi calls it Daqsus and present Tarsus; al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi and Alusi reconcile Ephesus as the former name with Tarsus as later name. Alusi says it was familiar home; Ibn Ashur calls it Ephesus. Al-Tha'labi's story spells Daphsus. Ibn al-Jawzī reports that some exegetes call it the youths' town and Muqātil names it Ephesus.
  18:19/q22/p2 Tarsus is the city's name. — reasons: Several sources state this directly without reconciling the older name.
  18:19/q22/p3 It was the city from which they fled; its specific name is unnecessary to the phrase. — reasons: Al-Tabrisi and Ibn Kathir identify it by relation to the youths; the Quran leaves the proper name unstated.
18:19/q23 Who or what does 'which of it' refer to? [أَيُّهَآ · referent] (turns on: Whether the city's people, its locations, or its foods are supplied to resolve the pronoun.)
  18:19/q23/p1 The city's inhabitants or vendors are understood: which person has the relevant food. — reasons: Al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas supply 'people'; al-Kashshaf compares 'ask the town' at 12:82; al-Nasafi, al-Samin, Bursevi and Tabatabai agree. Al-Tabari notes listeners understand food belongs to people.
  18:19/q23/p2 The pronoun can point directly to foods understood from context. — reasons: Al-Nahhas allows 'which food'; al-Samin says no elision is required; Abu Hayyan and Alusi present this alternative.
  18:19/q23/p3 It can refer grammatically to the city itself with an understood person or place. — reasons: Al-Tabari says the syntax attaches it to 'city' although the sense is inhabitants; Alusi lists city, residents, or food.
  18:19/q23/p4 It means which place in the city, such as a market stall. — reasons: Ibn Ashur makes place the referent and ṭaʿāman the specification of the comparative.
18:19/q24 How is 'let him look which has purer food' parsed? [فَلْيَنظُرْ أَيُّهَآ أَزْكَىٰ طَعَامًۭا · grammar] (turns on: The grammatical choice is interrogative versus relative ayyu and whether naẓar governs it or its clause.)
  18:19/q24/p1 Ayyuhā is an interrogative subject, azkā its predicate, and ṭaʿāman a specification. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj gives this parse; al-Wahidi cites Abu Ishaq; al-Razi and al-Nasafi follow; al-Samin and Alusi allow it. Al-Burhān reports al-Saʿdī's and grammarians' differing rules for a comparative annexed to its genus, then identifies azkā ṭaʿāman as a tamyīz construction scholars must explain within those rules. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the specification explicitly states the criterion of comparison, unlike an unqualified superlative.
  18:19/q24/p2 Ayy may be relative and function as the object, with an omitted predicate. — reasons: Abu Hayyan attributes this to Sibawayh; al-Samin and Alusi record the interrogative/relative options.
  18:19/q24/p3 The interrogative clause is what 'let him look' investigates. — reasons: Al-Akhfash says naẓar can be followed by a question without directly governing ayyu, illustrated with 'look, is Zayd more generous or Amr?'; al-Tabrisi calls the whole clause the object. Sībawayh says the interrogative clause in 'let him look which has purer food' occupies the verb's object position while retaining independent internal syntax, as at 18:12. He distinguishes direct government when no question intervenes, illustrates other embedded-question positions and accusative Arab usage, and notes that intransitive naẓar and asking about someone leave the name within the question. Al-Itqān says the exegete must attend to particles, nouns, verbs and adverbs because their varying uses alter meaning and inference.
  18:19/q24/p4 Naẓar can mean seeing or mental consideration. — reasons: Abu Hayyan states both senses.
18:19/q25 What does 'purest food' mean? [أَزْكَىٰ طَعَامًۭا · meaning] (turns on: Zakā can signify purity, increase, goodness or benefit; the context is disputed between lawful source, taste, quality, quantity and price.)
  18:19/q25/p1 Lawful, pure food, especially properly slaughtered meat from believers and free of idolatrous sacrifice. — reasons: Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abbas are repeatedly cited; al-Farra and al-Zajjaj explain that many townspeople were Magians, while hidden believers could slaughter lawfully. Al-Tabari prefers lawful food over mere abundance regardless of seller's stock. Ibn Kathir invokes 24:21 and 87:14 for purity and prefers wholesome purity. Reports also mention slaughtered pigs. Al-Damghānī glosses azkā in the sleepers' request as 'more lawful.'
  18:19/q25/p2 The more abundant food, or the vendor with the most food. — reasons: Ikrima gives the gloss; Abu Ubayda cites the seven-versus-three tribes line, repeated by al-Tha'labi; Ibn Qutayba derives it from increase. Al-Tabari accepts this Arabic usage but says it does not decide the context and prefers lawful purity.
  18:19/q25/p3 The tastiest, most pleasant, or wholesome food. — reasons: Muqatil, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi give taste; Ibn Kathir prefers a wholesome/pure sense supported by purification verses, while distinguishing it from mere quantity.
  18:19/q25/p4 The better or finest food in quality. — reasons: Qatada gives this repeatedly; Muqatil ibn Hayyan gives best quality. Alusi judges Qatada's reading best; Ibn Ashur argues zakā conveys increased goodness and benefit.
  18:19/q25/p5 The cheaper food or best value. — reasons: Ibn Qutayba lists low price; al-Mawardi, Ibn Jawzi and Yaman ibn Ri'ab give it, and al-Kashshaf, al-Nasafi, Baydawi and Bursevi include it.
  18:19/q25/p6 Lawful food specifically means food not stolen, extorted, usurped or bought with injustice. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj offers the source-of-property sense; Mujahid links it to an oppressive ruler's markets; al-Dahhak says much local property was seized. Abu Ishaq combines this with lawful slaughter; al-Wahidi states both.
  18:19/q25/p7 More blessed or fruitful food. — reasons: Abu Hayyan and al-Qurtubi preserve this gloss; Alusi says zakā's increase may be otherworldly reward from lawfulness or material benefit.
  18:19/q25/p8 A gloss transmitted as arfaḍ. — reasons: Al-Tha'labi ascribes the wording to Yaman b. Ri'ab without further explanation.
18:19/q26 What specific food did they seek or buy? [طَعَامًۭا · reports] (turns on: Reports name different foods while the verse keeps the noun general.)

Al-Wāḥidī requires witnessed transmission for occasions of revelation; Ibn Sīrīn reports ʿUbayda's warning that those who knew the occasions had gone.   18:19/q50/p2 The broader story includes a later encounter with the cave or its remains. — reasons: Al-Tabari reports Ibn Abbas passing a cave whose bones had vanished; Study Quran reports another account of preserved bodies after a renewed sleep.
  18:19/q50/p3 Christian accounts and Muslim reports partly overlap but differ on numbers, dog and duration. — reasons: Tabatabai says most historians place events between Jesus and Muhammad, outside the two Testaments, while Christian preservation was extensive; he compares Christian accounts with Ibn Ishaq's report.
18:19/q51 Where was the cave located according to later identifications? [* · reports] (turns on: Archaeological and historical fit is debated without decisive identification.)
  18:19/q51/p1 Rujayb near Amman is the strongest proposed fit, though identification remains unproved. — reasons: Tabatabai points to Jordanian excavation and some Muslim reports while stating no proposed cave has decisive evidence; he places Amman at ancient Philadelphia under Roman control until Muslim conquest.
  18:19/q51/p2 Other proposals place it near Damascus, Petra, Scandinavia or Nakhchivan. — reasons: Tabatabai lists Mount Qasiyun, Petra, seven preserved Roman-looking bodies in Scandinavia and a Caucasus cave; he objects that the northern claims conflict with the Roman setting and reach.
18:19/q52 How should differing transmitted recitations relevant to this verse be treated? [لَبِثْتُمْ بِوَرِقِكُمْ وَلْيَتَلَطَّفْ · readings]
  18:19/q52/p1 Transmitted variants are read as taught; dispute over an accepted reading is discouraged. — reasons: Ibn Masʿūd reports the Prophet rebuking a quarrel over a surah's verse count and directing readers to read as taught; Zayd ibn Arqam reports ʿAlī accepting the readings taught by Ibn Masʿūd, Zayd and Ubayy; ʿUmar reports the Prophet validating both his and Hishām's recitations and mentioning seven aḥruf.
18:19/q53 What is the form and etymology of 'the city'? [ٱلْمَدِينَةِ · meaning]
  18:19/q53/p1 Madīna has the faʿīla pattern and the plural mudun. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzī gives the morphological pattern and plural.
  18:19/q53/p2 It derives from dāna or dīn, denoting obedience or rule over inhabitants. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzī reports Qutrub deriving it from dāna; Ibn Fāris connects dīn with obedience to a governor or a people's subjection to a ruler. Ibn al-Jawzī cites dāna banī fulān and fī dīn fulān and lines of al-Nābigha and al-Ḥuṭayʾa for rule or subjection; a slave woman called madīna and al-Akhṭal's ibn madīna illustrate ownership and subduing.
18:19/q54 Why do the commands use fāʾ for the errand's steps but wāw for gentleness? [فَٱبْعَثُوٓا۟ فَلْيَنظُرْ فَلْيَأْتِكُم وَلْيَتَلَطَّفْ · rhetoric]
  18:19/q54/p1 Fāʾ orders dispatch, inspection and bringing food as successive steps; wāw adds gentleness because it is not a consequence of obtaining food. — reasons: Al-Burhān and al-Itqān explicitly contrast the ordered fāʾ clauses with the final wāw.
18:19/q55 What consonant articulation is prescribed when reciting words in this verse? [فَٱبْعَثُوٓا۟ وَلْيَتَلَطَّفْ · readings]
  18:19/q55/p1 The fāʾ before bāʾ is pronounced distinctly. — reasons: Ibn al-Jazarī prescribes clear fāʾ before mīm and wāw and, for most readers, before bāʾ, with one example of the latter.
  18:19/q55/p2 The lām of walyatalaṭṭaf is light in its ordinary pronunciation, though some manuals transmit an emphatic lām in this environment. — reasons: Ibn al-Jazarī directs readers to keep lām light, especially near emphatic letters, and names walyatalaṭṭaf; he also reports manuals with emphatic lām after certain silent emphatics or between emphatic letters, among their varying examples.
  18:19/q55/p3 Kāf should retain its strength and breathiness without a foreign voiceless sound or prolongation. — reasons: Ibn al-Jazarī gives this articulation rule especially for doubled kāf or adjacency to another breathy consonant.
18:19/q56 What principles permit broader lessons to be drawn from this narrative? [* · interpretation] (turns on: Whether general wording extends beyond its occasion and whether a secondary inference has a recognized basis.)
  18:19/q56/p1 A qualified reader may draw meanings grounded in Arabic usage, transmission and context, while retaining the plain sense and checking any further indication. — reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes reflective indication from direct denotation and recognized legal implications; he requires reliable transmission or qualified independent interpretation, warns against free-form preaching and esoteric claims, and says secondary senses accompany the primary. He illustrates contextually supported extension with ʿAmr's dry ablution, ʿUmar's land and calendar decisions, Ibn ʿAbbās's reading of Sūrat al-Naṣr, al-Shāfiʿī's consensus argument and divergent mutawātir readings. Al-Itqān favors applying general wording beyond its occasion and cites common Companion practice.
  18:19/q56/p2 A general verse's scope may be confined to its specific occasion unless separate evidence extends it. — reasons: Al-Itqān reports this restrictive view and notes agreed cases where verses remain limited to their causes.
